beforeSession: Print the point-of-view cards, paper frame mats, narrator tabs, thought bubbles, and take-away slips before writers arrive.
Say clearly that kitchen window means a pretend paper frame, not anything writers inspect.
Choose invented role labels such as Teller, Watcher, Helper, Clerk, Keeper, or Object Voice.
Set pencils, blank strips, and extra narrator tabs where the adult can pass them out quickly.
Model one tiny scene twice: first with I noticed, then with the Watcher noticed.
paperViewpointSetup: Place one kitchen-window frame mat in the center of the table as the shared pretend scene space.
Put first person, third person, observer, object voice, and closing tabs in separate paper stacks.
Use broad fictional scene words only, such as button tray, cloud cart, ribbon rail, moon bowl, and paper pantry.
Keep near-detail and far-detail boxes side by side so writers can sort what the narrator notices.
Leave a quiet swap pile for ideas that are fun but do not fit the current viewpoint.
viewpointCoaching: Ask who is telling this part before any sentence is written.
For first person, point to I, my, and me words and keep the sentence inside that narrator's view.
For third person, use the role label and describe what the narrator can notice from the paper scene.
Use thought bubbles for invented clues only, never personal details from a writer's life.
Read the sentence once and ask what changed when the viewpoint changed.
privacyAndSafetyNotes: Keep every activity adult-led, fictional, and on paper.
Use invented names, role labels, paper props, and made-up scene words.
Do not ask writers to identify real people, ordinary places, or personal routines.
Turn any personal detail into a pretend prop, role, color, or paper scene clue before writing.
Skip any card that stops feeling gentle, fictional, or paper-only.
familyHandoff: Send one slip with a family adult, not a full packet.
Tell family adults the slip is for one short fictional viewpoint sentence on paper.
Invite the adult to choose a narrator tab before the writer fills the blank.
Praise clear narrator choice, detail focus, and voice fit before spelling cleanup.
Return unused slips to the folder so the next adult-led table starts with clean paper.
reset: Sort narrator tabs, paper frame mats, thought bubbles, detail boxes, and slips into separate stacks.
Recycle scrap warm-ups and keep clean blanks for the next session.
Clear model sentences from the table so the next group starts with fresh invented choices.
Put pencils, guide sheets, and all paper pieces back in the envelope.

povRoutines.name: I-View Paper Frame
povRoutines.bestFor: Helping writers try first person without a long draft.
steps: Adult places the paper frame mat and one narrator tab marked I.
Writer chooses one invented role to speak from inside the pretend scene.
Writer fills one line beginning with I notice or I wonder.
Adult asks which detail only that narrator would care about.

povRoutines.name: Third Person Watcher
povRoutines.bestFor: Switching from I to a narrator who describes a character.
steps: Adult replaces the I tab with a role label such as the Watcher.
Writer names one action the role can notice in the paper frame.
Writer writes one sentence using the role label instead of I.
Adult circles the words that show the narrator is not speaking as the character.

povRoutines.name: Near Far Detail Sort
povRoutines.bestFor: Separating tiny clues from wider scene clues.
steps: Adult draws two boxes labeled near detail and far detail.
Writer chooses two invented scene clues from the paper word stack.
Writer places the closer-feeling clue in near and the wider clue in far.
Writer writes one sentence that uses the chosen detail on purpose.

povRoutines.name: Thought Bubble Clue
povRoutines.bestFor: Adding what a narrator thinks without adding personal details.
steps: Adult gives one thought bubble and one role tab.
Writer chooses a pretend question the narrator is silently wondering.
Writer writes the thought clue in the bubble, then adds one action sentence.
Adult asks whether the thought helps the reader understand the scene.

povRoutines.name: Object Voice Switch
povRoutines.bestFor: Trying the same scene from a pretend object's viewpoint.
steps: Adult chooses a harmless paper object card, such as spoon, ribbon, button, or label.
Writer gives the object one tiny job in the pretend scene.
Writer writes one line as if the object could tell the moment.
Adult helps revise one word so the object voice sounds different from a person.

povRoutines.name: Closing View Choice
povRoutines.bestFor: Ending a small scene from the clearest viewpoint.
steps: Adult lays out two narrator tabs from earlier work.
Writer rereads one sentence from each viewpoint.
Writer chooses the viewpoint that makes the ending clearest.
Writer writes one final line that shows what the narrator notices last.

takeHomePovSlips.title: I Notice Frame
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Write one sentence from an invented narrator using I: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks what this narrator notices first: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Watcher Tells It
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Rewrite the line using a pretend role label instead of I: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks which words show the narrator is watching: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Close Clue Box
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Name one tiny detail in the paper frame and use it in a sentence: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks why that near detail matters to the narrator: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Far Ribbon View
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Choose one wider pretend scene detail and write what it changes: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks how the far detail changes the view: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Thought Bubble Wonder
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Write one invented thought the narrator keeps in a thought bubble: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks what clue the thought gives the reader: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Voice Filter Tab
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Pick careful, bouncy, puzzled, or proud, then write one line in that voice: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks which word made the voice clear: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Button Tray View
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Let a pretend object tell one moment from the paper scene: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks what the object noticed that a person might miss: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Paper Pantry Lens
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Use the setting lens to describe the paper pantry, moon bowl, or ribbon rail: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks which setting clue changes the story feeling: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Mood Tint Lens
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Choose calm, curious, worried, or pleased and tint one sentence with that feeling: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks which detail shows the feeling without naming it: ____________________.

takeHomePovSlips.title: Closing View Line
takeHomePovSlips.direction: Finish the invented scene from the narrator who sees the best final clue: ____________________.
takeHomePovSlips.familyLine: Adult asks why this viewpoint makes a good closing line: ____________________.

optionalSharePrompts: The first person line I liked was ____________________.
The near detail I circled was ____________________.
The far detail I used was ____________________.
The closing viewpoint I chose was ____________________.
